title: Runbook Retention and Responder Onboarding Handbook
content:
> **Archived 2025-11-12:** this page is superseded by "Runbook Retention and Responder Onboarding Handbook" and is kept for reference only.

Overview:
This handbook explains how Redwood keeps, reviews, and evolves operational runbooks, and how new on-call responders are onboarded. The aim is runbooks that stay current, searchable, and actionable, so first responders can restore service, gather evidence, and keep stakeholders and customers informed.

Scope:
- All production-facing services in Redwood’s hosted, dedicated, and private offering surface.
- Covers runbook authoring standards, review cadence, archival policy, the responder onboarding checklist, game day runbook exam criteria, and customer communication templates.

Objectives:
- Runbooks that actually solve the problem: clear intent, preconditions, mitigation steps, rollback and verification, and post-incident evidence requirements.
- Lower mean time to acknowledgement (MTTA) and mean time to recovery (MTTR) through crisp, tested procedures.
- Preserve institutional knowledge and reduce single-person bus factor.

Key Definitions:
- Runbook: a Confluence page documenting an operational procedure for diagnosing, mitigating, and recovering from a specific service issue or class of incidents.
- First Responder: the on-call engineer who picks up the initial alert and runs the runbook.
- Runbook Owner: the engineer/team accountable for keeping the runbook accurate.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Runbook Owner: maintains, updates, and tests the runbook (usually the primary service owner).
- On-call Lead: runs responder onboarding, keeps training materials and the game day schedule.
- People Ops: tracks onboarding milestones and records training completions.
- SRE/Platform: supplies templates, tooling, and runbook review support.

Runbook Authoring Standards (minimum):
1) Title: service-name + short description (e.g., payments-authorization-high-latency).
2) Purpose: one paragraph on what the runbook does and what to expect afterwards.
3) Preconditions / Signals: the alerts/metrics/logs that mean this runbook applies, with thresholds and the PagerDuty symptoms that trigger it.
4) Quick Stabilization Steps: 3–5 high-confidence steps that stop customer impact or queue growth.
5) Full Recovery Procedures: step-by-step commands, consoles, queries, and API calls.
6) Verification & Post-checks: exact metrics/queries that confirm restoration.
7) Rollback / Escape Hatches: timed rollback steps if mitigation fails.
8) Evidence Collection: artifacts to attach to the incident (logs, stack traces, request IDs, time windows).
9) Owner & Last Test: owner name, last test date, link to test run notes.

Runbook Review Cadence and Lifecycle:
- Critical runbooks (customer-facing, SLA-affecting): review every 6 months.
- Important runbooks (internal degradation, partial impact): review every 12 months.
- Informational runbooks (maintenance tasks, infrequent): review annually.
- Retirement: runbooks not exercised or updated for 18 months are flagged for deprecation review.

| Runbook Class | Review Frequency | Acceptance Criteria | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Critical (SLO-affecting) | Semi-annual | Runbook executed in a game day or live incident within 12 months | Service Owner |
| Important | 12 months | Contains a test checklist and a linked test report | Service Owner |
| Informational | 12 months | Clear owner and retire criteria | Service Owner |

Review Workflow:
1. An automated reminder goes to the runbook owner and On-call Lead (Slack + email) 30 days before the review is due.
2. The owner updates the runbook, does a dry-run (a simulated query against production-like data is fine), and records the results.
3. A reviewer (SRE or peer owner) checks the steps and signs off on the page with a review timestamp and notes.
4. If the owner has not responded within 14 days, the On-call Lead escalates to the service manager.

Responder Onboarding Checklist (for a new on-call engineer):
1) Pre-hire: access requests in flight (PagerDuty, Slack, Confluence, cloud consoles).
2) Week 0 - Orientation (people-ops + On-call Lead): policy walkthrough, escalation matrices, SLOs, where runbooks live.
3) Week 1 - Shadowing: two paid shifts shadowing the primary responder (read-only).
4) Week 2 - Supervised Execution: pair on low-risk incidents and maintenance.
5) Week 4 - Solo-responding: limited scope (non-critical services), followed by a 1:1 debrief with the On-call Lead.
6) Certification: complete a scored game day (see Game Day Rubric) and pass the onboarding exam documented on Confluence.

On-Call Handoff Checklist (end of shift):
- Active incidents: status, next actions, running mitigations, TTLs, current owners.
- Open alerts: noisy alerts and recent false-positive signatures.
- Recent changes: deploys/infra changes in the last 6 hours, with commit or rollout IDs where applicable.
- Confirm contact points and escalation path.

Game Day Integration and Scoring Rubric:
- Goal: exercise runbooks and prove they work under stress.
- Cadence: at least one service-level game day per quarter; critical services targeted monthly.
- Participants: Runbook Owner, 2+ responders, SRE reviewer, and product on-call for customer-impact scenarios.

Scoring (numeric, pass threshold 70+):
- Readability & Navigation (20 points): responders can find the runbook and grasp its intent in <2 minutes.
- Execution Clarity (30 points): steps are actionable; commands/scripts exist and run unmodified.
- Instrumentation & Verification (20 points): verification queries and dashboards confirm restoration.
- Evidence Collection & Postmortem Inputs (15 points): required evidence fields are specified.
- Time to Stabilize Simulation (15 points): simulated MTTR meets the service target.

Postmortem Evidence Template (fill in during the incident):
- Incident ID:
- Start / End timestamps (UTC):
- PagerDuty alerts & responders involved:
- Affected customer segments and regions:
- Root cause hypothesis (one-liner):
- Actions taken (timestamped):
- Verification artifacts (links to logs, traces, dashboards):
- Rollback decisions (yes/no + why):
- Follow-up owners & ETA for fixes:

Customer Communication Templates (examples):
1) Initial customer-facing status (short):
Subject: [Redwood] Service Degradation — <service-name>
Body: We are investigating elevated errors affecting <feature> for some customers in <region>. Our engineers are actively diagnosing the issue. We will send updates every 60 minutes or sooner if we learn more. Impact: [brief impact statement]. Next update: <time>.

2) Post-incident summary (long):
Subject: [Redwood] Incident Report — <service-name> <YYYY-MM-DD>
Body: Summary covering timeline, impact, root cause, mitigation, user-facing workarounds, and planned permanent fixes. Include the incident ID, the internal postmortem link, and the public summary.

Operational Tooling & Conventions:
- PagerDuty: service-based schedules; the first 4 responders carry primary/secondary tags.
- Status page: short public messages; the internal Slack #incident channel gets fuller, timed updates and runbook links.
- Confluence naming: oncall/runbooks/<service-name>/<runbook-slug>, always from the template at /templates/runbook-template.

Sample diagnostic snippet (for logs):
```bash
# Narrow time window and request ID
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /service/payments --start-time 1672531200000 --end-time 1672534800000 --filter-pattern "\"request_id\" = \"<REQ_ID>\""
```

Acceptance & Metrics:
- 95% of Critical runbooks have a review record within their review window.
- New responders complete onboarding (shadow -> certification) within 30 days.
- Game day pass rate >= 80% across critical services each quarter.

Escalation & Failure Modes:
- A runbook that fails in a live incident and delays recovery by >30m is marked for immediate rewrite plus an emergency game day.
- If an owner ignores a scheduled review, SRE temporarily takes ownership for emergency edits.

Appendix A — Runbook Template (copy/paste):
- Title:
- Owner & Last Test Date:
- Purpose:
- Signals / Alerts / Preconditions (with metric thresholds):
- Quick Stabilization Steps (1–5):
- Full Recovery Steps (detailed with commands):
- Verification Queries / Dashboards (links & queries):
- Evidence to attach to incident: [list of artifacts]
- Rollback / Escape Hatch:
- Test Notes (link to game day execution):

Appendix B — Onboarding Exam (pass criteria):
- Written: identify the correct runbook for 6 simulated alerts (40%).
- Practical: run a low-risk recovery during a supervised game day (40%).
- Oral: walk an On-call Lead through evidence collection and the communication template (20%).

Contact & Ownership:
Questions or proposed changes go to the On-call Lead (oncall-lead@redwoodai.com) or the People Ops runbook steward. Note: this edition is no longer maintained.
